statement: Regular polygon $P$ has twice as many sides as regular polygon $Q$. Each interior angle of $P$ is $30^\circ$ larger than each interior angle of $Q$. What is the measure of each interior angle of $P$?

choices.misconception: I solved and found that Q is a hexagon, then I gave the interior angle of Q, 120 degrees, instead of the angle of P.
I found that P has 12 sides and computed 360 divided by 12 = 30, but that is the exterior angle of P, not the interior angle.
I found that P has 12 sides and computed (12 - 2) times 180 = 1,800, which is the sum of all the interior angles, not one angle.

hints: It is easier to compare exterior angles. How is an exterior angle of a regular $n$-gon related to $n$?
If $Q$ has $n$ sides, its exterior angle is $\frac{360}{n}$ and the exterior angle of $P$ is $\frac{360}{2n}$. A larger interior angle means a smaller exterior angle, by the same $30^\circ$.
$\frac{360}{n} - \frac{360}{2n} = \frac{180}{n} = 30$, so $n = 6$ and $P$ has $12$ sides. Its exterior angle is $30^\circ$, so its interior angle is $180^\circ - 30^\circ$.

solutions.reliable: Let $Q$ have $n$ sides, so $P$ has $2n$ sides. Each interior angle of a regular $k$-gon is $180 - \frac{360}{k}$. The condition is $\left(180 - \frac{360}{2n}\right) - \left(180 - \frac{360}{n}\right) = 30$, which simplifies to $\frac{180}{n} = 30$, so $n = 6$. Then $P$ has $12$ sides and each interior angle is $180 - \frac{360}{12} = 150^\circ$. Check: $Q$ is a hexagon with interior angle $120^\circ$, and $150 - 120 = 30$.
solutions.elegant: Doubling the number of sides halves the exterior angle. The exterior angle drops by half of its value, and that drop is $30^\circ$, so $Q$'s exterior angle is $60^\circ$ and $P$'s is $30^\circ$. Each interior angle of $P$ is $180^\circ - 30^\circ = 150^\circ$.
